steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Algorithmic management is a term that describes certain labor management practices in the contemporary digital economy. In scholarly use, the term was first coined in 2015 by Min Kyung Lee, Daniel Kusbit, Evan Metsky, and Laura Dabbish, who used it to describe the managerial role that algorithms play on the Uber and Lyft platforms. Since then other scholars have taken it up to describe the managerial and organisational characteristics of platform economies more generally. But digital direction of labor was already present in manufacturing since the 1970s, and algorithmic management is becoming more and more widespread across a wide range of industries.

Broadly, the concept of algorithmic management can be defined as delegating managerial functions to algorithmic and automated systems. Algorithmic management was enabled by "recent advances in digital technologies", which allow real-time and "large-scale collection of data", and this data is then used to "improve learning algorithms that carry out learning and control functions traditionally performed by managers". The term does not refer to one specific underlying technology. It covers the design choices, organisational policies, and governance that surround the managerial use of algorithms in workplaces.

- Accounting devices
  - firms use ecology of accounting devices: [quote: "rankings, lists, classifications, stars and other symbols..." without traditional hierarchical control]
  - many fall under algorithmic management; first developed by sharing/gig economy companies; labor and cost-cutting measures

  - five typical features:

    - real-time responsiveness to data informing management decisions

cited_draft
steps.text:
Algorithmic management is a term that describes certain labor management practices in the contemporary digital economy. In scholarly use, the term was first coined in 2015 by Min Kyung Lee, Daniel Kusbit, Evan Metsky, and Laura Dabbish, who used it to describe the managerial role that algorithms play on the Uber and Lyft platforms.[1,2] Since then other scholars have taken it up to describe the managerial and organisational characteristics of platform economies more generally.[3,4] But digital direction of labor was already present in manufacturing since the 1970s, and algorithmic management is becoming more and more widespread across a wide range of industries.[5]

Broadly, the concept of algorithmic management can be defined as delegating managerial functions to algorithmic and automated systems.[6] Algorithmic management was enabled by "recent advances in digital technologies", which allow real-time and "large-scale collection of data", and this data is then used to "improve learning algorithms that carry out learning and control functions traditionally performed by managers".[7] The term does not refer to one specific underlying technology. It covers the design choices, organisational policies, and governance that surround the managerial use of algorithms in workplaces.[8,9]

Firms in the contemporary workplace use an ecology of accounting devices, such as "rankings, lists, classifications, stars and other symbols' in order to effectively manage their operations and create value without the need for traditional forms of hierarchical control."[10] A lot of these devices fall under the label of algorithmic management. They were first developed by companies in the sharing economy or gig economy, where they worked as effective labor and cost-cutting measures.[11] For example, the explainer of the term by Data&Society[12] describes algorithmic management as 'a diverse set of technological tools and techniques that structure the conditions of work and remotely manage workforces.[11] Data&Society also gives a list of five typical features of algorithmic management:

Prolific data collection and surveillance of workers through technology;

Real-time responsiveness to data that informs management decisions;

Automated or semi-automated decision-making;

Transfer of performance evaluations to rating systems or other metrics; and

The use of "nudges" and penalties to indirectly incentivize worker behaviors.[11]

People who support algorithmic management say that it "creates new employment opportunities, better and cheaper consumer services, transparency and fairness in parts of the labour market that are characterised by inefficiency, opacity and capricious human bosses."[13] Critics of algorithmic management, on the other hand, say that the practice causes several issues, especially in how it impacts the employment status of the workers who are managed by its new array of tools and techniques.[2,14,15]
